tagline: River valleys, a railway depot and roads inherited from the Yellowstone Trail.
intro: The Cascade Valleys Heritage Corridor follows SR 202 from Woodinville to North Bend through the Sammamish and Snoqualmie valleys. The drive moves from wineries and city streets to Patterson Creek, a crossing of the Snoqualmie River and a long hairpin over Tokul Creek. Designated a state scenic and recreational highway, it is promoted by State of Washington Tourism for valley scenery, outdoor recreation and cultural history. The tourism office lists a 30-mile drive taking one hour.

The Seattle, Lake Shore and Eastern Railway built its Bothell–North Bend line in 1889; by 1902, wagon roads ran beside it. The Redmond–North Bend road joined the Yellowstone Trail in the 1910s, including a section near Redmond paved in brick in 1913. Numbered highways came later: the Woodinville–North Bend road became part of SR 522 in 1964 and carried the SR 202 designation by 1970.

From Woodinville, travel south through the Sammamish River valley to Redmond and the edge of Marymoor Park near Lake Sammamish. Continue beside Patterson Creek toward Fall City, cross the Snoqualmie River, and follow it southeast to Snoqualmie Falls. Beyond downtown Snoqualmie, the Three Forks lowlands lead to North Bend beneath Mount Si. In North Bend, SR 202 turns southwest onto Bendigo Boulevard through downtown, crosses the South Fork again, and finishes at Interstate 90.

moments.title: Snoqualmie Falls
moments.text: Snoqualmie Falls drops 268 feet between Fall City and Snoqualmie. For the Snoqualmie People, the falls are central to culture, belief and spirituality. The Snoqualmie Indian Tribe purchased the falls, Salish Lodge and surrounding property in 2019, halting a proposed development. The purchase followed the Tribe’s 2015 Save Snoqualmie Falls campaign and its opposition to development near the falls and burial grounds. Most river water is diverted into two power plants, the first built underground in 1899 and the second downstream in 1910. When the river runs high enough, water crosses the whole precipice and the falls form a curtain.
moments.notice: During high water, the falls spread into a curtain across the precipice.

moments.title: Northwest Railway Museum, Snoqualmie
moments.text: Scrollwork beneath the depot’s broad eaves gives a freight-and-passenger station an unusually decorative face. The Seattle, Lake Shore and Eastern built it in 1890 to serve local products bound for Seattle and vacationers coming to Snoqualmie Falls. A projecting bay held the telegrapher’s office, and the north end is semicircular. The museum’s heritage railway incorporates 5.5 miles of the original 1889 line. Staff and volunteers train in historic operating practices, including methods from before two-way radios. The restoration workshop uses carpentry and machining equipment to make parts that have been out of production since the 1960s.
moments.notice: Look for the depot’s semicircular north end and scrollwork where its wooden braces meet the eaves and pillars.

moments.title: North Bend
moments.text: Mount Si towers over North Bend, a familiar shape from the opening credits of Twin Peaks. The series was partly filmed in town. The mountain and neighboring Little Si take their names from homesteader Josiah “Uncle Si” Merritt. The main Mount Si trail climbs 3,500 feet over four miles to the summit ridge; reaching the summit itself requires an exposed scramble up the block called the Haystack. Little Si is a separate mountain, divided from Mount Si by a valley and reached from a different trailhead. The state owns the mountain land and protects it as a Natural Resources Conservation Area.
